newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia rates surge after Negara warning.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia rates surge after Negara warning.

text.p: Malaysian interbank rates surged on Thursday after a central bank warning that it would take tough measures, including raising interest rates, to stamp out speculation in the ringgit, money market dealers said.

Bank Negara governor Ahmad Mohamed Don said on Wednesday Malaysia would use all means possible to defend its currency, which has been under pressure from overseas selling in the wake of a crisis in the Thai baht.
The benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) was fixed at 8.38 percent at 0300 GMT, against 7.92 percent on Wednesday.
The one-month KLIBOR was fixed at 9.0 percent against 8.0 percent on Wednesday.
KLIBOR is fixed by taking an average of rates offered by various banks in the country.
One-month money was offered as high as 10.0 percent, dealers said.

Dealers said the rise in interbank rates was also triggered by an expected liquidity squeeze as a result of Bank Negara's massive intervention in the foreign exchange market on Tuesday to help the ringgit.
Although the actual size of the intervention was not known, dealers said it could mop up anything from 2.5 billion to 5.0 billion ringgit ($1-2 billion) from the system.
Settlement of Tuesday's intervention will be on Thursday.
"Bank Negara warning and market tightness had a combined effect on rates. The question now is how high rates will go," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank.
The overnight interbank rate, which traded between 8.0 and 9.5 percent on Wednesday, was expected to rise sharply later on Thursday.
"The overnight should be in double-digit," the dealer said.

Ahmad said the central bank had been in the process of normalising interest rates to levels which had prevailed before its intervention in the foreign exchange market in May following a speculative attack on the Thai baht.
"Now we have no choice but to allow the rates to go up again," he said in an interview with Bernama news agency.

In May, Bank Negara intervened heavily to defend the ringgit, causing a sudden tightening of liquidity in the banking system and pushing interbank rates to unusually high levels. The intervention mopped up around four billion ringgit from the system, dealers said.
Interbank rates rose to as high as 20 percent then.
Dealers said the market was also concerned that Bank Negara would re-impose capital controls to broaden its intervention tools.
In 1994, faced with an attack on the ringgit, Bank Negara imposed negative interest rates on foreign deposits, banned swaps and stopped foreigners from buying Malaysian government paper.
Dealers said the current interbank market trend, if allowed to continue, would squeeze local corporates and possibly lead to another round of increases in banks' base lending rates (BLR).
Banks had raised their BLR by an average 30 basis points after the jump in interbank rates in May. Most banks are now quoting BLRs at 9.60 percent.
Under a new formula announced in October 1995, the BLR is pegged to the average three-month KLIBOR over a month.
The central bank then fixes a ceiling rate.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
